summary: Extends the File Transfer Protocol to support multiple character sets and languages, with recommendations for proper internationalization of file names and messages.

plainLanguage.summary: FTP used to understand mostly English letters. This lets it carry file names in many writing systems and languages.

questions: how does ftp handle utf-8 file names
what is the ftp lang command
how do ftp clients detect utf-8 support
what is the ftp feat utf8 line
subtitle: How FTP learned to carry file names in any script and to speak the user's language, without breaking old clients.

tldr.problem: FTP was built around 7-bit ASCII, so file names and server messages could not reliably carry characters from the world's other writing systems or languages.
tldr.mechanism: Pathnames are sent as UTF-8, which matches ASCII for plain characters, servers announce this with the FEAT line UTF8, and a new LANG command lets the client pick the language of server messages.
tldr.outcome: Old ASCII-only clients can still talk to new servers, while new clients and servers can exchange international pathnames. The RFC updates RFC 959.

today: RFC 2640 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 959, and no newer RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its UTF-8 pathname rules and the LANG command are the part of FTP this document defines.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed Internationalization
sections.content:
RFC 959 defines FTP around 7-bit ASCII. As the Internet spread, the need to handle characters outside ASCII and Latin-1 became urgent. The RFC sets a hard constraint: the fix must not break the large installed base of existing clients and servers.

The document does three things. It removes the 7-bit restriction on pathnames in commands and server responses. It RECOMMENDS the Universal Character Set (ISO/IEC 10646) in its UTF-8 form. And it defines a new LANG command for language negotiation. It follows the IETF policy on character sets and languages in RFC 2277.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP only knew a tiny alphabet, and there were millions of old programs using it. The goal was to teach it more letters without making the old programs stop working.

sections.title: One Character Set and UTF-8
sections.content:
The RFC picks a single shared character set instead of asking every system to convert between many. For FTP that set SHALL be ISO/IEC 10646:1993, and clients and servers are STRONGLY RECOMMENDED to use UTF-8 when exchanging pathnames. The contents of files are not touched: there is no obligation to convert data for operations such as STOR or RETR.

How a server stores files stays a local decision. Before pathnames are exchanged they SHOULD be converted to ISO/IEC 10646 and UTF-8 encoded.

UTF-8 writes each character as 1 to 6 bytes. A one-byte sequence always starts with a zero bit, so ASCII characters look identical in UTF-8. In longer sequences the count of leading one bits in the first byte gives the length, and each continuing byte starts with the bits 10. Because other character sets rarely look like valid UTF-8, a simple routine can check whether a name is valid UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: UTF-8 is a code where plain English letters stay exactly as they were, and other letters take a few extra bytes. That is why old programs still understand the plain parts.

sections.title: Pathname Rules
sections.content:
FTP commands that carry a pathname look like COMMAND SP pathname CRLF. Many operating systems allow spaces, carriage returns and line feeds inside names, which would confuse parsing. The RFC redefines a pathname as 1*(%x01..%xFF) and adds rules:

  • There MUST be exactly one SP between the command and the pathname. Any further spaces belong to the pathname, so in STOR SP SP SP foo.bar the name is two spaces followed by foo.bar.
  • A CR inside a pathname MUST be padded with a NUL before sending, and the receiver MUST strip that NUL. This follows the Telnet approach in RFC 854.
  • Conforming clients and servers MUST support UTF-8 for pathnames. Names that are valid UTF-8 are assumed to be UTF-8; the character set of any other name is undefined.
  • If a name cannot be converted to a usable code set, UTF-8 SHOULD be kept to avoid data loss. If the encoding cannot be determined, the raw bytes SHOULD be used.

Implementations that pad 3-letter commands such as CWD to a fixed 4 characters are non-compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: File names may contain spaces and odd characters. The rules say exactly where the name starts and how to mark special characters, so the server never splits a name in the wrong place.

sections.title: Detecting UTF-8 with FEAT
sections.content:
Servers MUST report UTF-8 support in response to the FEAT command from RFC 2389. The feature is a line containing the string UTF8, which is not case sensitive but SHOULD be sent in upper case. Feature lines must be indented by one space.

Clients MUST support FEAT and recognize UTF8 to learn whether a server does UTF-8. For servers that do not, how the client behaves is a quality of implementation issue: it MAY assume some other encoding, ask the user, or remember a guess for later sessions. A client that cannot display a character is RECOMMENDED to show the octets in URL %HH form, though it MAY use question marks or hexadecimal values instead. Glyph rendering itself is out of scope.

Mirror servers MAY store and present the exact pathname bytes they received from the main server.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the fancy letters, the client asks the server what it can do. If the server says UTF8, both sides know they can use them.

sections.title: The LANG Command
sections.content:
The new LANG command tells the server which language to use for greetings and the explanatory text of responses. Its parameter is a language tag from RFC 1766; with no parameter the server's default language is used. Greetings before negotiation use the default language, which the RFC RECOMMENDS be English in ASCII. Once a language is negotiated, the server MUST send text in that language, encoded in UTF-8.

Only the human-readable text changes. FTP commands and numeric reply codes are protocol elements and are never translated, and data on the data connection is not translated either.

A client MAY send LANG at any time, but SHOULD do so before authentication. To help a server tell new clients from old ones, a client MUST send HOST and/or LANG before any other command except FEAT. Until a server sees one of them, it SHOULD assume the client does not follow this specification. Sending HOST or REIN undoes the effect of LANG.

Replies: 200 means success, 501 a badly formed argument, 504 a well-formed but unimplemented one, and 500 or 502 from older servers that do not know the command. A server that supports only a variant such as en-UK may answer a request for en-AU with 200 and switch to the closest variant.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like telling a waiter which language you would like the menu in. The dishes keep their numbers, but the words next to them change to your language.

sections.title: Advertising Languages in FEAT
sections.content:
A server that supports LANG MUST add a feature line to its FEAT response: LANG followed by a list of supported language tags separated by semicolons. At least one tag MUST be listed, and an optional asterisk marks the language currently in use. The single leading space is required.

For example, LANG EN*;FR means English and French are supported and English is active. After the client sends LANG fr and receives 200, a new FEAT shows LANG EN;FR*.
sections.plainLanguage: The server posts a list of the languages it speaks and puts a star next to the one it is using right now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is brief. It says the document addresses character sets beyond one byte and a new language negotiation command, and that conformance to it should not induce a security risk.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors think these changes do not make FTP less safe, and they say so in a single short note.

SWITCHING LANGUAGE, AS IN THE RFC EXAMPLE

data.title: FEAT and LANG exchange
data.code:
C> feat
S> 211- <any descriptive text>
S>  ...
S>  LANG EN*;FR
S>  ...
S> 211 end
C> LANG fr
S> 200 Le response sera changez au francais
C> feat
S> 211- <quelconque descriptif texte>
S>  ...
S>  LANG EN;FR*
S>  ...
S> 211 end
